stories.working_title: Agents for Humans: Making a Strands approval survive process death
stories.deck: A human-in-the-loop agent is only useful if the question survives longer than the process that asked it. LastTake separates the suspended Strands session from authoritative run state, then makes absence and model failure block rather than pass.

sections.heading: The hard part begins after the agent asks
paragraphs: LastTake checks a fictional shoot-day package before a production-to-post handoff. The Strands orchestrator calls bounded tools for coverage, continuity, media identity and rights, then hands their saved findings to deterministic eligibility policy. It cannot approve a pickup, approve a wrap or turn missing evidence into a pass.

Both human approval tools accept a Strands ToolContext and interrupt the run. A request may be answered after the Lambda invocation that created it has disappeared. Treating that pause as an in-memory callback would make the human step decorative: the question would exist only while the original process remained warm.

sections.heading: Two stores, two different responsibilities
paragraphs: The deployed architecture deliberately does not rebuild run state from S3. Aurora DSQL is the run-state store for findings, decisions, delivery outcomes and review state. Strands S3SessionManager stores the suspended agent session needed to resume the interrupted tool call. S3 also holds supplied artifacts and write-once receipts, but it is not the deployed run-state database.

That distinction matters during recovery. The HTTP handler constructs a new WrapRun over Aurora DSQL and a new Strands Agent over the existing S3 session. The resumed tool body starts again from its beginning, and ToolContext.interrupt returns the saved answer. Any outward effect therefore sits after the interrupt and behind a content-derived idempotency boundary.

sections.heading: A process boundary is an assertion the deployment must prove
paragraphs: A local test creates a fresh Agent object over the persisted session and confirms that the approval resumes and routes the accepted request once. That proves reconstruction, but it does not prove Lambda process death or the AWS storage adapters.

The deployment workflow closes that gap. It starts the checkpoint, records the pending interrupt and serving container, changes the Lambda configuration so existing execution environments retire, verifies that the health endpoint still reports Aurora DSQL, and submits the approval in a later request. The gate refuses to pass unless the second response comes from a different container and the resumed workflow reports an accepted delivery outcome. This draft describes the gate; the published article must link the exact successful deployment run for its source commit.

sections.heading: Fail closed when the reader disappears
paragraphs: Durable pause and resume solve only the transport problem. The eligibility result also has to remain conservative when an interpreter fails. Expected checks are derived from the package, not from whichever findings an agent happened to return. A missing result is therefore an exception rather than an implicit pass.

On the synthetic corpus, `PYTHONPATH=src python tools/ablation.py` reports that the normal offline reader supports coverage for 31 of 34 required beats, while the deliberately unreachable reader supports 0 of 34. All 31 affected beats become unknown rather than passing. Those figures describe this fixed fictional package and this command only; they are not an accuracy score or a comparison with another product.

sections.heading: What I would carry into another agent
paragraphs: Persist the agent continuation and business state explicitly, and do not describe them as the same thing. Put external effects after an interrupt, make replay observable, and use a stable idempotency key. Then derive required work independently of the model so a missing tool result cannot erase a requirement.

LastTake still has important boundaries. The public browser uses a scripted planner and offline lexical interpreter; Amazon Bedrock is exercised separately. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore is not deployed. The role selector is a demo control, not staff authentication. The records are synthetic, and no human-time or production-benefit study has been run.

stories.working_title: Agents for Humans: Proving EventBridge consumption without claiming editorial action
stories.deck: An accepted PutEvents call proves that EventBridge accepted an entry. LastTake adds a separate terminal Lambda and a content-bound S3 receipt to prove that a subscriber consumed it, while refusing to call that editorial work.

sections.heading: Acceptance is not consumption
paragraphs: LastTake publishes domain events for checkpoints, findings, approvals and turnover. The publisher can record whether EventBridge accepted or rejected an entry, but acceptance does not prove that a target received it. Calling that downstream completion would turn a transport acknowledgement into a workflow claim.

The solution is a separate EventBridge rule whose target is a dedicated delivery-recorder Lambda. The subscriber is terminal by design: it validates the envelope, records consumption and stops. It has no EventBridge publish permission, imports no orchestrator builder and never starts or resumes Strands. The Strands workflow starts synchronously from the HTTP request path.

sections.heading: Bind the receipt to the bytes that arrived
paragraphs: The recorder checks the EventBridge source, domain event type, schema, canonical identifiers, payload shape and the content-derived idempotency key before writing anything. A valid receipt carries the domain event id, EventBridge transport id and time, correlation id, digest of the domain detail, Lambda request id, consumption time and deployed commit SHA. It deliberately omits the event payload.

The S3 key is derived from the correlation and domain event ids. PutObject uses `IfNoneMatch: *`, so a duplicate delivery cannot overwrite the first observation. A byte-identical redelivery returns the original receipt. A colliding domain id with a different transport identity or digest is surfaced as an error rather than hidden as a duplicate.

sections.heading: Make the proof visible without broadening it
paragraphs: The History API reads receipts only under the requested correlation prefix and joins one to an event only when schema, subscriber, event id, event type, correlation id and detail digest all match. Until then the interface says `not_observed`, because asynchronous absence is not proof of delivery failure. After a match it says the EventBridge subscriber consumed the event and shows the recorder identity and transport metadata.

That label is intentionally narrow. It proves that the configured rule invoked the recorder and the recorder stored a matching receipt. It does not prove that editorial acted, that an email or payment occurred, that a handoff was accepted, or that EventBridge triggered an agent.

sections.heading: Test the code path and the deployed wiring
paragraphs: The source tests cover valid storage, duplicate delivery without overwrite, collision refusal, malformed envelope rejection, configured-bucket use, absence of an event-publish or orchestrator path, and correlation-scoped reads. Those tests exercise the contract without pretending to be AWS delivery evidence.

The deployment workflow separately asks CloudFormation for the rule and recorder, verifies that the rule target is the dedicated Lambda, polls the product event history, and requires a consumed receipt whose deployed SHA matches the candidate. The published story must cite the exact successful run for the linked commit; source code alone is not evidence that the current AWS release delivered an event.

sections.heading: Boundaries that remain
paragraphs: The public demo uses fictional production records, a scripted planner and an offline lexical interpreter. Amazon Bedrock is tested through a separate deployment path and is not active in the public browser. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore is not deployed. Demo-role selection is not staff authentication.
No human benefit, delivery-time improvement or production outcome has been measured. The receipt proves a bounded infrastructure fact and nothing beyond it.

stories.working_title: Agents for Humans: Offline review without replaying a human mutation
stories.deck: LastTake keeps a bounded, tab-scoped view and an unsent draft through a disconnect. Reconnect reads authority from the server; it never turns offline state into a queued approval or an automatic write.

sections.heading: Offline is a trust-boundary decision
paragraphs: A script supervisor may lose connectivity while reviewing a scene. Preserving context is useful, but replaying a decision after the evidence changed is not. LastTake therefore implements bounded offline review rather than general offline synchronization.

The service worker caches only the application shell and built assets. API, health, acceptance and UAT responses bypass the cache. The application stores one last-confirmed workspace snapshot and one unsent evidence draft in sessionStorage, scoped to the exact session and run. The draft also records the package revision on which it was prepared. Malformed, mismatched or oversized values are ignored.

sections.heading: A cached view is never authority
paragraphs: During a disconnect the saved snapshot is labelled read-only. Creating a run, recording a decision, answering an approval and saving evidence remain disabled. If a mutation loses its response, the interface marks the outcome unknown and does not retry it automatically.

Reconnect performs fresh reads for the session and selected run. If the authoritative package revision differs from the draft or prior snapshot, writes stay disabled and the changed digests are shown for review. Only an explicit review action rebases the draft. The person may then choose to save it, producing a new request rather than a replay of the earlier attempt.

sections.heading: The browser journey checks the negative space
paragraphs: The end-to-end journey saves a draft, confirms the shell cache, disconnects, verifies read-only state, changes the server revision through a separate client, reconnects, requires revision review and finally saves once. Its request counter is as important as the visible screen: no ingest request occurs while offline or during reconnect, and one occurs only after review and an explicit click.

This is not a queue, conflict-free replicated data type or background merge. It does not cache API responses, replay approvals or decisions, synchronize across tabs, or promise that every browser can reload a document under every automation protocol.

sections.heading: State the WebKit harness limit instead of hiding it
paragraphs: The Chromium journey exercises a full top-level reload from the cached shell while the browser context is offline. Playwright WebKit rejects an offline top-level navigation in its protocol layer before a controlling service worker can answer, so the WebKit branch does not claim that document-reload proof.

The WebKit branch still inspects the real shell cache and exercises the live disconnect, read-only workspace, authoritative reconnect, revision-review barrier and no-replay request count. This separates a product assertion from a harness limitation: cached-document reload is proved in Chromium, while the remaining recovery contract is exercised in WebKit.

sections.heading: What this demo does and does not establish
paragraphs: The feature demonstrates a conservative recovery path over fictional records. It does not establish full offline operation, authenticated staff authority or production readiness. Demo roles are not staff authentication, and a stored draft is not a saved production record.

The public path uses the real Strands SDK with a scripted planner and offline lexical interpreter. Amazon Bedrock runs only in a separate deployment check, Amazon Bedrock AgentCore is not deployed, and no footage or audio is analysed. Human-time and quality benefits remain unmeasured.
